title: The common good (CCC 1905–1912)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy and sin: the Gospel reveals mercy first, and sin comes into view inside it. Your line was mercy first. Did you manage to put something down? Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

A streetlight at the corner. Nobody owns it. Nobody thanks it. But a nurse walking home from a late shift can see the curb, a kid can find the way back from a friend's house, and an old man can take his dog out without tripping. Next to it: a crosswalk, a water fountain in the park, a library with its doors open, a bus that runs on time. None of these makes anyone happy, exactly. They just make it possible for a lot of different people to get on with their lives. When one goes dark, everyone on the street feels it. The Catechism has a name for that whole web of things that belong to nobody and serve everybody.
screen: `A STREETLIGHT NOBODY OWNS.` → `A CROSSWALK, A LIBRARY, A BUS.` → `WHEN ONE GOES DARK.`

segments.voice: The phrase is the common good. The Catechism says that because people are social by nature, the good of each person is bound up with the good of all. Then it gives a definition, borrowed from the Second Vatican Council: the common good is the sum of the social conditions that allow people, as groups and as individuals, to reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily. Notice the word conditions. The common good isn't a society deciding what will make each person happy. It's the streetlight, not the walk home. It makes the flourishing possible, and leaves the living to the people. The Catechism names three essential parts. First, respect for the person. Public authorities are bound to respect the basic rights of the human person, including the freedom to act by a sound conscience, the protection of privacy, and rightful freedom in matters of religion. Second, social well-being and development. What a truly human life needs should be within reach: food, clothing, health, work, education and culture, suitable information, the right to start a family. Third, peace: the stability and security of a just order. The Catechism then widens the circle. Because the human family is one, there is also a universal common good, reaching across borders. It mentions refugees and migrants by name, and migrants' families. And it ends with a reminder that keeps the idea honest: the order of society must always serve the good of persons, not the other way around. It quotes Jesus from Mark: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Systems exist for people.
screen: `THE GOOD OF EACH, BOUND TO ALL.` · `CONDITIONS, NOT A SCRIPT FOR HAPPINESS.` · `RESPECT, WELL-BEING, PEACE.` · `A UNIVERSAL COMMON GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something for everyone's benefit. Settle, and breathe. Walk in your mind through the places you'll pass today: a sidewalk, an office kitchen, a shared hallway, a group chat, a park. Look for one thing that belongs to nobody and serves everybody, and that could use a hand. Litter by a bench. A broken light someone should report. A sink full of shared mugs. A newcomer nobody has said hello to. Choose one. Picture yourself doing it, without anyone noticing. If you pray, you can offer it for the people who'll never know. The bell holds the time.
Common good. The social conditions that let people, together and one by one, reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily: respect for the person, well-being, and peace. Today's word.
Your line: everyone flourishing. Today, do the one thing you chose for the shared space, and leave it a little better than you found it. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: The common good is a central idea of Catholic social teaching, and the Church's documents invoke it when they speak about work, charity, civic life and politics.

fork.setup: you sit on a neighborhood board. an empty lot can become parking reserved for the board's own shops, a small park open to everyone, or stay fenced off. which fits the common good as the Catechism describes it?

leave it fenced; no one loses.
fork.reveal: the common good is conditions that let everyone flourish, not the good of a few, and not nothing at all.
